subtopic_detail: Radio-opaque foreign body ingestion where the number of objects changes the urgency
stem:
You are the emergency department registrar. A 3 year old boy is brought in two hours after his mother saw him spit out and then swallow some of the small silver balls from his older brother's desk toy. She thinks he swallowed two or three.

He is playing in the cubicle, is not drooling, and has just finished a cup of juice without difficulty. His chest is clear and his abdomen is soft and non tender with normal bowel sounds. The abdominal radiograph shows two round radio-opaque objects lying in the gastric shadow, stacked against each other with a thin lucent line between them.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 108, blood pressure 96/60, respiratory rate 22, SpO2 99 per cent on room air, temperature 36.6
data_table.Examination: No drooling, tolerating oral fluids, chest clear, abdomen soft and non tender
data_table.Investigations: Abdominal radiograph shows two round radio-opaque objects in the gastric shadow, apposed with a thin lucent line between them and no free gas

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Discharge home with advice to sieve the stools and repeat the film in a week
options.rationale: Watchful waiting with stool checking is the pathway for a single blunt object such as a coin in the stomach of a well child, and it is unsafe once more than one magnetic object is present (Source: RCH CPG: Foreign Body Ingestion).

options.text: Give oral polyethylene glycol and repeat the abdominal film in 24 hours
options.rationale: Accelerating transit does not separate objects that are already held together across tissue, and the delay allows pressure necrosis of the bowel wall to progress (Source: RCH CPG: Foreign Body Ingestion).

options.text: Arrange urgent upper endoscopy for retrieval of both objects tonight
options.rationale: Two or more magnets attract across loops of bowel and cause pressure necrosis, fistula and perforation, so while they remain within endoscopic reach in the stomach they are removed urgently even though the child is well (Source: RCH CPG: Foreign Body Ingestion).

options.text: Observe on the ward with four hourly review and a film in the morning
options.rationale: Observation wastes the window in which the objects are still retrievable from above, and clinical signs of bowel injury appear only after necrosis is established (Source: RCH CPG: Foreign Body Ingestion).

options.text: Refer for laparotomy and removal of both objects with bowel inspection
options.rationale: Open surgery is the answer once the objects have passed the duodenum and cannot be reached endoscopically, or when there are peritoneal signs, and neither applies while they sit in the stomach (Source: RCH CPG: Foreign Body Ingestion).

explanation.summary: Ingested foreign bodies are triaged by what the object is, where it sits and whether the child has symptoms, and the number of objects is decisive when they are magnetic. A single blunt object in the stomach can be managed expectantly, whereas two or more magnets, or one magnet with another metallic object, can trap bowel wall between them and cause necrosis within hours. Button batteries lodged in the oesophagus form the other emergency, needing removal within two hours because of alkaline mucosal injury. The apposed pair with a lucent gap between them on the film is the radiographic signature that should trigger the call to the endoscopist.
key_points: One blunt object in the stomach of a well child can be managed expectantly
Two or more magnets are an emergency regardless of symptoms
Objects in the stomach are removed endoscopically, beyond the duodenum surgically
A lucent gap between apposed radio-opaque objects suggests interposed tissue
An oesophageal button battery needs removal within two hours
explanation.pearls: Two magnets anywhere in the gastrointestinal tract mandate removal on the day of presentation, and if they have already passed the ligament of Treitz the decision moves from endoscopy to surgical review rather than to observation.

subtopic_detail: Return to contact sport after concussion in a person under 19 years
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 14 year old boy eight days after he collided head to head in a junior rugby league match. He did not lose consciousness but was dazed on the field, was removed from play, and had headache and difficulty concentrating in class for four days.

He has now been free of headache, fogginess and light sensitivity for three full days, has returned to a full school day, and has completed light jogging and stationary cycling without symptoms. His neurological examination including balance testing is normal. His coach has asked you to sign him off for the semi final this Saturday, and his father says he has never had a previous head knock.

data_table.Examination: Normal cranial nerve, limb and cerebellar examination, tandem gait normal, no neck tenderness
data_table.Timeline: Injury day 0, symptoms resolved day 5, aerobic exercise tolerated days 6 to 8, currently day 8

lead_in: What is the most appropriate advice about returning to play?

options.text: Allow return to contact training now with a full game on the weekend
options.rationale: Clearing him at day eight applies the adult community pathway, and the paediatric pathway is deliberately slower because of the longer physiological recovery in the developing brain (Source: Australian Concussion Guidelines for Youth and Community Sport).
source_refs: Australian Concussion Guidelines for Youth and Community Sport

options.text: Arrange a computed tomography head scan before any return to training
options.rationale: Imaging answers the question of structural injury in the acute phase and has no role in return to play decisions in a boy who is now asymptomatic with a normal examination (Source: Australian Concussion Guidelines for Youth and Community Sport).
source_refs: Australian Concussion Guidelines for Youth and Community Sport

options.text: Allow return once he completes a two day graded exercise progression
options.rationale: Tolerating the graded exercise stages is necessary but not sufficient in this age group, because a minimum calendar interval also applies before contact is resumed (Source: Australian Concussion Guidelines for Youth and Community Sport).
source_refs: Australian Concussion Guidelines for Youth and Community Sport

options.text: Withhold competitive contact sport until at least 21 days after injury
options.rationale: The Australian youth pathway sets a floor of 21 days from injury before competitive contact or collision sport, with at least 14 symptom free days first, and non contact conditioning continues in the meantime (Source: Australian Concussion Guidelines for Youth and Community Sport).
source_refs: Australian Concussion Guidelines for Youth and Community Sport

options.text: Refer for neuropsychological testing before clearing him to play again
options.rationale: Formal neuropsychological assessment is reserved for persisting symptoms beyond four weeks or repeated concussions, and it does not shorten the minimum interval in an uncomplicated first concussion (Source: Australian Concussion Guidelines for Youth and Community Sport).
source_refs: Australian Concussion Guidelines for Youth and Community Sport

explanation.summary: Australian community and youth sport guidance deliberately separates the child and adolescent pathway from the professional pathway, because young athletes recover more slowly and repeat injury during the vulnerable window carries disproportionate risk. Return to learn comes before return to sport, and the graded exercise progression only starts once symptoms have settled. Even a straightforward recovery cannot compress the minimum calendar interval to competitive contact play. Any return of symptoms at a stage means dropping back to the previous stage rather than pushing through.
key_points: Return to learn precedes return to sport in school aged athletes
Symptom resolution alone does not authorise a return to contact
The Australian youth floor is 21 days from injury before competitive contact sport
At least 14 symptom free days are required before contact training
Neuroimaging has no role in return to play decisions
explanation.pearls: A community athlete under 19 cannot return to competitive contact sport sooner than 21 days after concussion in Australia, even with complete symptom resolution by day five, and non contact aerobic conditioning is what fills the interval.

sources.label: Australian Concussion Guidelines for Youth and Community Sport

subtopic_detail: Choice of imaging for suspected hip dysplasia once the femoral head has begun to ossify
stem:
You are the paediatric outpatient registrar seeing a 6 month old girl referred because her mother noticed that the skin creases on her thighs do not match. She was born at term in the breech position and had a normal newborn hip examination documented in her blue book.

She is not yet crawling but rolls both ways and sits with support. On examination the left hip abducts to only 45 degrees while the right abducts fully, the left knee sits lower than the right when the hips and knees are flexed with the feet together, and there is no click or clunk on provocative testing. Her leg lengths and spine are otherwise normal.

data_table.Examination: Limited left hip abduction to 45 degrees, asymmetric thigh creases, positive Galeazzi sign on the left, no clunk on Ortolani or Barlow testing
data_table.History: Breech presentation at term, newborn hip examination recorded as normal, no family history of hip disease

lead_in: What is the most appropriate imaging investigation?

options.text: Arrange static and dynamic hip ultrasound of both hips this week
options.rationale: Ultrasound is the modality of choice under about four months, but from four to six months the ossifying femoral head casts an acoustic shadow over the acetabulum and makes measurements unreliable (Source: RCH CPG: Developmental Dysplasia of the Hip).
source_refs: RCH CPG: Developmental Dysplasia of the Hip

options.text: Arrange an anteroposterior pelvis radiograph and orthopaedic review
options.rationale: Once the femoral head ossifies at around four to six months the plain anteroposterior pelvis film becomes the reliable test, and limited abduction with a positive Galeazzi sign warrants orthopaedic assessment alongside it (Source: RCH CPG: Developmental Dysplasia of the Hip).
source_refs: RCH CPG: Developmental Dysplasia of the Hip

options.text: Apply a Pavlik harness and review in the orthopaedic clinic in three weeks
options.rationale: Harness treatment is applied after imaging confirms the diagnosis and its success falls sharply beyond six months of age, so it is not started blind at this visit (Source: RCH CPG: Developmental Dysplasia of the Hip).
source_refs: RCH CPG: Developmental Dysplasia of the Hip

options.text: Reassure and reassess the hips at the twelve month health check
options.rationale: Limited abduction is the most reliable sign of dysplasia after the newborn period, and deferring to twelve months risks presentation with an established dislocation and a limp (Source: RCH CPG: Developmental Dysplasia of the Hip).
source_refs: RCH CPG: Developmental Dysplasia of the Hip

options.text: Request magnetic resonance imaging of both hips under light sedation
options.rationale: Magnetic resonance imaging is used to assess reduction after closed or open reduction, not to make the initial diagnosis, and it requires sedation for no additional information here (Source: RCH CPG: Developmental Dysplasia of the Hip).
source_refs: RCH CPG: Developmental Dysplasia of the Hip

explanation.summary: A normal newborn hip examination does not exclude dysplasia, because the acetabulum can become progressively dysplastic over the first months and breech presentation remains the strongest single risk factor. The physical signs shift with age: instability signs such as Ortolani and Barlow fade after about three months, and asymmetric abduction with a positive Galeazzi sign takes over. Imaging must follow the same clock, with ultrasound early and plain radiography once the ossific nucleus appears. Late diagnosis matters because harness treatment fails beyond six months and the child then faces closed or open reduction with a spica cast.
key_points: Breech presentation at term is the strongest risk factor even with a normal newborn examination
Ortolani and Barlow signs become unreliable after about three months
Limited abduction and a positive Galeazzi sign are the older infant signs
Ultrasound is the test under four months, plain radiography from about four to six months
Pavlik harness success falls away after six months of age
explanation.pearls: Hip ultrasound loses accuracy once the femoral ossific nucleus appears at around four to six months, so a six month old with asymmetric abduction is imaged with an anteroposterior pelvis radiograph rather than repeat ultrasound.

sources.label: RCH CPG: Developmental Dysplasia of the Hip
Australian Commission on Safety and Quality in Health Care: DDH

subtopic_detail: Nocturnal events in a preschooler where the pattern separates seizure from parasomnia
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar reviewing a 4 year old girl referred by her general practitioner with a working diagnosis of night terrors. Her parents have kept a two week diary and have filmed several events on a phone.

The diary records six to eight events on most nights, spread from shortly after she falls asleep through to the early morning. Each lasts about 30 seconds and looks identical to the last: she opens her eyes, stiffens her right arm, then cycles her legs and makes a grunting noise. Her parents can rouse her at the end and she talks to them normally before going back to sleep. She is tired and irritable during the day, and her development and examination are normal.

data_table.Examination: Normal neurological and developmental examination, no neurocutaneous stigmata, head circumference on the 50th centile
data_table.Sleep diary: Six to eight stereotyped events per night lasting about 30 seconds, occurring throughout the night, with full alertness immediately afterwards

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Reassure, advise a safe sleep environment, and review in three months
options.rationale: Reassurance suits a parasomnia, which occurs once or twice a night in the first third of sleep, varies between episodes and leaves the child confused rather than immediately alert (Source: RCH CPG: Sleep Problems).

options.text: Start melatonin 2 mg at bedtime and review the sleep diary in one month
options.rationale: Melatonin addresses delayed sleep onset rather than events arising out of established sleep, and it would delay recognition of an epilepsy syndrome (Source: RCH CPG: Sleep Problems).

options.text: Arrange overnight oximetry and refer for adenotonsillectomy assessment
options.rationale: Obstructive sleep apnoea causes snoring, witnessed pauses and restless sleep with daytime tiredness, but not brief identical motor events with preserved awareness afterwards (Source: RCH CPG: Obstructive Sleep Apnoea).

options.text: Refer for polysomnography to quantify arousals from slow wave sleep
options.rationale: Polysomnography maps sleep architecture and respiratory events, and while video is useful it is not the test that identifies interictal epileptiform discharges (Source: RCH CPG: Afebrile Seizures).

options.text: Refer for a sleep deprived electroencephalogram and neurology review
options.rationale: High frequency, brief, stereotyped hypermotor events occurring throughout the night with rapid recovery of awareness point to a sleep related epilepsy, and the sleep deprived recording is the investigation that captures the discharges (Source: RCH CPG: Afebrile Seizures).

explanation.summary: The nocturnal event history is discriminating if the right five questions are asked: how many per night, when in the night, how long, how similar to each other, and how the child behaves immediately afterwards. Parasomnias are infrequent, arise from slow wave sleep in the first third of the night, last minutes, vary between episodes and end in confusion with amnesia. Sleep related hypermotor seizures are brief, numerous, identical, distributed across the whole night and followed by preserved awareness. Daytime irritability from fragmented sleep is common to both and does not discriminate. Home phone video has become one of the most valuable pieces of evidence in this assessment.
key_points: Count the events per night and note their distribution across the night
Stereotypy between events is the single most useful feature for seizure
Immediate return of awareness after an event argues against a parasomnia
Parasomnias arise from slow wave sleep in the first third of the night
Home video should be actively requested and reviewed
explanation.pearls: More than two identical events in a single night, each under a minute and spread across the whole night, moves a child from the parasomnia pathway to a sleep deprived electroencephalogram rather than to reassurance.

subtopic_detail: Bowed legs with a metabolic bone profile that separates nutritional from inherited rickets
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar seeing a 20 month old boy referred because his legs have become increasingly bowed since he started walking at 17 months. His family moved to Melbourne from a country with a warmer climate two years ago, his mother covers most of her skin outdoors, and he was breastfed without supplementation until 14 months.

He now drinks about 1.2 litres of cow milk each day and eats little else. He has no family history of bone disease and both parents have straight legs. On examination he has symmetrical bowing of both tibiae, widening at both wrists, and a normal chest and abdomen.

data_table.Examination: Symmetrical genu varum, widened wrists, no frontal bossing, no proximal weakness, growth tracking on the 25th centile
data_table.Investigations: Corrected calcium 2.15 mmol/L (2.20-2.60); phosphate 0.85 mmol/L (1.20-1.80); alkaline phosphatase 1180 U/L (100-400); parathyroid hormone 18.5 pmol/L (1.6-6.9); 25 hydroxyvitamin D 16 nmol/L (greater than 50)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Start cholecalciferol and oral calcium with repeat bloods in one month
options.rationale: A low 25 hydroxyvitamin D with a raised parathyroid hormone identifies nutritional deficiency, and a child on high milk intake with poor solid variety still needs calcium alongside replacement to avoid the hypocalcaemia that follows bone healing (Source: RCH CPG: Vitamin D Deficiency).

options.text: Start cholecalciferol alone and repeat the bone profile in three months
options.rationale: Replacing vitamin D without calcium in a child with a poor dietary calcium intake risks symptomatic hypocalcaemia as remineralising bone takes up circulating calcium (Source: RCH CPG: Vitamin D Deficiency).

options.text: Refer for genetic testing for X linked hypophosphataemia before treating
options.rationale: Inherited phosphate wasting gives a low phosphate with a normal 25 hydroxyvitamin D and a normal or only mildly raised parathyroid hormone, so the markedly raised parathyroid hormone and deficient vitamin D here point elsewhere (Source: RCH CPG: Vitamin D Deficiency).

options.text: Refer to orthopaedics for bracing of both legs and monitor his growth
options.rationale: The bowing is a consequence of soft undermineralised bone and straightens with medical treatment, so bracing addresses the deformity while leaving the cause untreated (Source: RCH CPG: Vitamin D Deficiency).

options.text: Advise increasing cow milk to two litres daily and review in one month
options.rationale: Cow milk is not fortified with vitamin D in Australia, and volumes at this level displace iron rich solids and cause iron deficiency anaemia (Source: NHMRC Infant Feeding Guidelines).

explanation.summary: Nutritional rickets remains common in Australian children with darker skin, limited sun exposure, prolonged unsupplemented breastfeeding and a monotonous diet. The biochemistry separates the causes efficiently: a low 25 hydroxyvitamin D with secondary hyperparathyroidism is nutritional, whereas a low phosphate with normal vitamin D and normal parathyroid hormone suggests renal phosphate wasting. Alkaline phosphatase is the most sensitive marker of active disease and is what falls first with successful treatment. The maternal vitamin D status should be checked at the same time, because the mother of an affected breastfed child is usually deficient herself.
key_points: Raised alkaline phosphatase with a raised parathyroid hormone signals active nutritional rickets
Give calcium with vitamin D when dietary calcium intake is poor
Cow milk in Australia is not fortified with vitamin D
Milk volumes above about 500 mL daily displace iron rich solids
Screen and treat the mother of an affected breastfed infant
explanation.pearls: Alkaline phosphatase falls before the radiographic changes resolve, so a repeat level at four weeks is the earliest objective sign that cholecalciferol and calcium replacement is working.
